title: Concurrency models
summary: Threads, processes, and asyncio: what the GIL serializes, when each model wins, and the one rule of the event loop.

clips.title: The GIL
clips.question: Why don't threads speed up CPU-bound Python code?

scenes.say: Python concurrency, question one. Why don't threads speed up CPU-bound Python code? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: Why don't threads speed up CPU-bound Python?

scenes.say: The global interpreter lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. Thread one holds it, while the others wait. The interpreter switches the holder every few milliseconds, but only one ever runs, so CPU-bound work gets no faster with more threads. Blocking I/O is different. A thread waiting on the network releases the lock, so another thread can run in the meantime. That is why threads do help I/O-bound work.

steps.note: One thread runs bytecode at a time
Thread 1 holds the GIL; 2 and 3 wait
Switch interval (~5 ms): a new holder
Still one at a time: no CPU speedup
Thread 1 waits on the socket, GIL released
Another thread runs during the wait

clips.title: Threads, processes, or asyncio
clips.question: When do you choose threads, processes, or asyncio?

scenes.say: Question two. When do you choose threads, processes, or async I O? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: Threads, processes, or asyncio: when do you pick each?

scenes.say: Threads are preemptive OS threads sharing one interpreter. They suit moderate I/O-bound work, but give no speedup on CPU. Processes each get their own interpreter and their own GIL, so CPU-bound work runs truly in parallel. The cost is heavier startup, and pickling arguments across the boundary. Async I O runs one thread and one event loop, switching only at await. It scales to thousands of sockets, but gives no CPU speedup either.

items.label: threading
items.title: I/O-bound, moderate
items.body: Shared memory; GIL blocks CPU speedup.

items.label: multiprocessing
items.title: CPU-bound
items.body: One GIL per process; arguments are pickled.

items.label: asyncio
items.title: I/O-bound, massive
items.body: One thread, cooperative switches at await.

scenes.say: The primes benchmark makes it concrete. Checking big numbers for primality with a thread pool takes about as long as doing it sequentially. A process pool divides the time by the number of cores.

left.label: ThreadPoolExecutor
left.title: ≈ sequential time
left.code:
with ThreadPoolExecutor() as ex:
    list(ex.map(is_prime, NUMBERS))
# the GIL serializes is_prime
left.body: Real threads, but one runs Python at a time.

right.label: ProcessPoolExecutor
right.title: ÷ number of cores
right.code:
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
    list(ex.map(is_prime, NUMBERS))
# one interpreter + GIL per process
right.body: is_prime must be a top-level, picklable function.

clips.title: The rule of asyncio
clips.question: What does await do, and what is the cardinal rule of asyncio?

scenes.say: Question three. What does await actually do, and what is the one rule of async I O? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: What does await do, and what's the rule of asyncio?

scenes.say: Create task schedules the spinner on the event loop. Awaiting the slow coroutine hands control back to the loop, so the spinner animates in the meantime. When the result arrives, cancel stops the spinner by raising cancelled error inside it.

props.title: Cooperative switching at await
props.code:
async def spin(msg):
    for char in itertools.cycle("|/-\\"):
        print(f"\r{char} {msg}", end="", flush=True)
        try:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)   # yield to the loop
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            break

async def supervisor():
    spinner = asyncio.create_task(spin("thinking!"))
    result = await slow_work()          # loop runs spin meanwhile
    spinner.cancel()
    return result

highlights.note: create_task: schedule spin on the loop
await: give control back to the loop

scenes.say: That leads to the cardinal rule: never block the event loop. A coroutine that calls time dot sleep freezes every task on the loop, and the spinner stops dead. Await async I O dot sleep instead, or push blocking calls to a thread with to thread.

left.label: Blocks
left.title: Every task stops
left.code:
async def slow_work():
    time.sleep(3)        # blocks the thread
    return 42

right.label: Yields
right.title: Loop keeps running
right.code:
async def slow_work():
    await asyncio.sleep(3)   # yields to the loop
    return 42
# or: await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_call)

verdict.text: Blocking work goes to a thread or a process.

scenes.say: To recap. The GIL lets one thread run Python at a time, but I/O releases it. Use threads for moderate I/O, processes for CPU-bound work, and async I O for massive I/O. And never block the event loop.

items.text: The GIL: one thread runs bytecode; I/O releases it.
asyncio for massive I/O—never block the loop.
